chapters.title: Chapter 4: Related Parties and Capital Allocation

lessons.title: Dividends, Buybacks and Idle Cash: How Minority Shareholders Are Treated

body.text: Cash that reaches every shareholder equally is the only return a minority shareholder is guaranteed to share. How a company returns cash, or refuses to, tells you whose money management thinks it is.

children.text: The last lesson covered where management reinvests cash. This one covers the other side: what happens to cash that is not reinvested. A company can pay dividends, buy back shares, or keep the cash on its balance sheet. All three can be perfectly sensible. But dividends and buybacks are also where minority shareholders finally get something in hand, and idle cash is money that is technically yours but controlled entirely by someone else. The choices management makes here are some of the most honest signals of how it views minority shareholders.

A dividend is paid to every shareholder in exact proportion to their holding. There is no way to give the promoter more per share than you get. That makes dividend history a clean test of whether profits eventually reach minority shareholders. Since dividend distribution tax was abolished in 2020, dividends are taxed in shareholders' hands at their applicable income tax rates, with TDS deducted when dividends from a company exceed ₹10,000 in a financial year.

body.latex: \text{Dividend Payout} = \frac{\text{Total Dividends}}{\text{Net Profit}} \qquad \text{Cash Return Ratio} = \frac{\text{Dividends} + \text{Buybacks}}{\text{Free Cash Flow}}
body.caption: Measure both over five years; free cash flow = operating cash flow minus capex

children.text: Payout ratio against profit can mislead, because profit is not cash. The cash return ratio against free cash flow is the better test. A company paying out 60% of profit but only 20% of free cash flow is hoarding. A company paying out 60% of profit when its free cash flow is barely positive may be paying dividends it cannot afford, sometimes to meet the cash needs of a promoter.

body.label: A useful public benchmark
body.value: Infosys: return up to 85% of free cash flow over five years
body.context: Infosys has published a capital allocation policy committing to return a stated share of free cash flow through dividends and buybacks. A written, measurable policy lets shareholders hold management to account.

children.text: Buybacks: Useful, but Read the Fine Print

In a buyback, the company buys its own shares and extinguishes them. Shareholders who sell get cash; those who stay own a bigger share of the company. Unlike dividends, buybacks do not treat everyone identically. Who participates, at what price, and through which route all decide who benefits.

body.caption: Key buyback rules for Indian listed companies

cells: Up to 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves; up to 10% needs only board approval, above that a special resolution
Debt to equity must not exceed 2:1 after the buyback
No fresh buyback offer within one year of the previous one closing
Tender offer, where shareholders tender shares at a fixed price. SEBI phased out buybacks through the stock exchange's open market route, which ended from April 2025
15% of a tender offer is reserved for small shareholders, those holding shares worth up to ₹2 lakh on the record date
Can participate in tender offers, and must disclose their intention to do so in the offer document

For buybacks from 1 October 2024, the amount received is taxed in shareholders' hands like a dividend, and the cost of the shares tendered can be claimed as a capital loss. Earlier, the company paid buyback tax and shareholders received the proceeds tax free

body.text: The 2024 tax change matters for governance reading. Before it, buybacks were often the most tax-efficient way for promoters in high tax brackets to take cash out, which could make a buyback look more generous to minorities than it really was. With buyback proceeds now taxed like dividends, a company choosing a buyback over a dividend has to justify it on valuation, not tax.

children.text: When Does a Buyback Actually Help Remaining Shareholders?

A buyback uses cash that was earning interest to retire shares that were earning profit. It raises EPS only if the company's earnings yield, the inverse of its P/E, is higher than the after-tax return it was earning on that cash. Take an illustrative company with ₹1,000 crore of profit, 50 crore shares, EPS of ₹20, and cash earning 5% after tax. It spends ₹2,000 crore on a buyback.

body.caption: The same ₹2,000 crore buyback at two different prices

children.text: The same buyback is good for remaining shareholders at ₹250 and bad at ₹500. A buyback announced when the stock trades at a very high multiple, especially with a large premium to the market price, can transfer value from the shareholders who stay to those who sell. If the promoter is among the sellers, that is a minority treatment question, not just a valuation one.

body.title: Is This Buyback Accretive?
body.prompt: A company has net profit of ₹800 crore and 40 crore shares, so EPS is ₹20. It spends ₹1,500 crore of cash, which was earning 5% after tax, to buy back shares at ₹300 each. What is EPS after the buyback? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Shares bought = ₹1,500 crore ÷ ₹300 = 5 crore, leaving 35 crore shares. Interest lost = ₹1,500 crore × 5% = ₹75 crore, so profit falls to ₹725 crore. EPS = ₹725 crore ÷ 35 crore = ₹20.71, up about 3.6%. It is accretive because the earnings yield at ₹300 is 6.67% (₹20 ÷ ₹300), above the 5% the cash was earning.

body.title: The Buyback Rule of Thumb
body.textWithBlank: A buyback raises EPS for remaining shareholders only if the company's earnings yield is higher than the ___ return it was earning on the cash used.
body.explanation: Earnings yield (EPS ÷ price) is what the company 'earns' by retiring a share. The after-tax return on cash is what it gives up by spending the cash. If the second is bigger, the buyback lowers EPS.

children.text: Tata Consultancy Services has run several large tender offer buybacks alongside regular dividends, including a ₹17,000 crore buyback in 2023 at ₹4,150 per share. Its promoter, Tata Sons, participated in these offers. Because tender offers have a 15% small shareholder reservation and acceptance is proportionate within each category, retail holders could tender on the same terms as the promoter. This is what a well-structured buyback looks like: disclosed in advance, open to all, and part of a consistent cash return record rather than a one-off event.
Idle Cash: Your Money, Their Control

Some Indian companies accumulate cash for years with no stated purpose. A buffer for a cyclical business or a planned expansion is reasonable. A pile that keeps growing, with low payouts and no plan, has two costs. It drags down returns, and it sits in the control of management and the promoter, available for acquisitions, group company loans, or pet projects that shareholders never approved.

Illustration: a company has ₹10,000 crore of equity. ₹6,000 crore runs the operating business, earning 30% after tax, or ₹1,800 crore. The other ₹4,000 crore sits in cash and deposits earning 5% after tax, or ₹200 crore.

body.title: ROE with and without ₹4,000 crore of idle cash (%)

children.text: With the cash kept, profit is ₹2,000 crore on ₹10,000 crore of equity, a 20% ROE. Return the cash and profit is ₹1,800 crore on ₹6,000 crore, a 30% ROE. The operating business is identical. The only difference is ₹4,000 crore of shareholder money earning a deposit rate inside the company.

Idle cash can be changed by shareholder pressure. By 2017, Infosys had built up a very large cash balance, and former senior executives, including former CFO Mohandas Pai, publicly urged the company to return more of it. Later that year Infosys announced its first ever buyback, of ₹13,000 crore, and went on to adopt the written capital return policy mentioned earlier.

body.text: Check where the cash actually is. 'Cash and investments' on the balance sheet can include inter-corporate deposits with group companies, investments in unlisted group entities, or fixed deposits pledged against group borrowings. Read the notes on investments, loans, and other bank balances before assuming a cash pile is really available to shareholders.

body.title: Fair vs Unfair Treatment of Minority Shareholders

columns.label: Fair
points: A written, measurable capital return policy
Dividends that track free cash flow over time
Tender offer buybacks at reasonable valuations, open to all on equal terms
Cash held for a stated purpose, with a timeline
Surplus returned when no good reinvestment exists

columns.label: Unfair
points: Cash piling up for years with minimal payouts and no plan
Dividends cut or skipped while promoter pay keeps rising
Buybacks at very high valuations that mainly let the promoter exit
'Cash' that turns out to be deposits with group companies
Large dividends paid despite weak cash flow, apparently to fund a pledged promoter

body.title: Which Cash Return Is Least Fair?
body.question: Which of these capital return decisions is least fair to minority shareholders?
options: An IT services company with no debt pays out 80% of free cash flow as dividends every year
A consumer company runs a tender offer buyback at a 10% premium when the stock trades at 14 times earnings, with the promoter choosing not to participate

A company whose promoter has 60% of their stake pledged announces a tender offer buyback at 55 times earnings and a 25% premium, with the promoter tendering the maximum allowed, funded by new borrowing
A cyclical steel company keeps a large cash buffer during a downturn and explains it will resume dividends when steel prices recover
body.explanation: Option C combines several problems. At 55 times earnings, the buyback almost certainly reduces EPS for remaining shareholders. The large premium transfers value to sellers. The promoter, who needs cash because of the pledge, is the biggest seller. And the company is borrowing to fund it, weakening the balance sheet that remaining shareholders own. The other options are consistent payouts, a sensible buyback, or a stated reason for holding cash.

body.title: The Cash-Rich Company That Never Pays
body.scenario: A family-controlled auto ancillary company listed on NSE has a market cap of ₹12,500 crore. Its balance sheet shows ₹5,000 crore of 'cash and investments', about 40% of market cap. It has paid a dividend of ₹2 per share, a payout ratio of about 8%, for five straight years while net profit doubled. Over the same period, remuneration to three promoter family executives rose by 150%. The investments note shows ₹1,800 crore of the ₹5,000 crore is in inter-corporate deposits with two promoter group companies, and ₹600 crore is in an unlisted group real estate venture. Management says the cash is being 'conserved for future growth opportunities' but has not announced any expansion plan.
body.prompt: What does this tell you about how minority shareholders are treated, and what would you want the company to do?
body.modelAnswer: Minority shareholders are being treated as an afterthought. First, the real idle cash is not ₹5,000 crore. ₹2,400 crore, nearly half, is already deployed with promoter group entities through deposits and an unlisted real estate investment, which are related party exposures, not liquid cash. Second, a flat ₹2 dividend and an 8% payout while profit doubled means almost all of the extra profit stayed under promoter control. Third, promoter pay rising 150% while dividends stayed flat shows the family is taking its share of the growth through salaries, which minorities cannot share in. 'Conserving for growth' with no plan is not a capital allocation policy. As a shareholder, you would want the group company deposits recalled and the real estate investment explained or exited, a written capital return policy linked to free cash flow, a meaningful dividend increase or a fairly priced tender offer buyback, and independent directors to explain why these exposures were approved. Until then, value the company excluding the ₹2,400 crore of group exposures and apply a governance discount to the rest of the cash.

body.title: Check How One of Your Holdings Treats Minority Shareholders
steps: On screener.in, note dividend payout ratio for the last ten years and whether it moves with profit
From the cash flow statement, add up dividends and buybacks for five years and divide by cumulative free cash flow
Check whether the company has a written capital allocation or dividend distribution policy, which top listed companies must publish, and whether it has followed it
For any buyback, note the price, P/E at announcement, premium to market, and whether the promoter tendered shares
Compare cash and investments with market cap, then read the investments and loans notes to see how much is actually with group companies
Compare the growth in dividends per share with the growth in promoter remuneration over five years

body.text: Companies and individuals named in this lesson are discussed based on public disclosures and widely reported events, for education only. Tax rules are summarised at a high level and can change; confirm current rules before acting. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security or tax advice.

points: Dividends are the fairest distribution because every shareholder receives the same amount per share; measure payouts against free cash flow, not just profit
Buybacks do not treat shareholders identically: price, route, premium, and promoter participation decide who benefits
A buyback raises EPS only when the earnings yield exceeds the after-tax return on the cash used; the same buyback was accretive at ₹250 and dilutive at ₹500
Since 1 October 2024, buyback proceeds are taxed like dividends in shareholders' hands, and the open market buyback route ended from April 2025
Idle cash lowers returns, cutting ROE from 30% to 20% in the illustration, and remains under the promoter's control
Always check whether 'cash' is really deposits or investments with group companies, and compare dividend growth with promoter pay growth
